questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A transit planner has a fixed budget of 100 buses and must serve both a growing suburb and an aging downtown. What economic problem does this illustrate?

options.text: Efficiency, because any allocation automatically maximizes ridership
Inflation, because demand for transit always raises operating costs
options.misconception: treats a resource limit as a price-level problem

options.text: Scarcity, because available buses cannot satisfy every desired route at once
options.misconception: confuses scarcity with a temporary shortage of vehicles

options.text: Growth, because the fleet size will expand without new funding
options.misconception: assumes resources grow on their own

questions.explanation: The fixed fleet relative to competing needs is scarcity. Efficiency is the goal, but scarcity is the underlying condition; inflation and automatic growth are unrelated.
questions.hint: Look for the condition of limited means versus unlimited wants.

provenance.author: bank-team-macroeconomics
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The board's report shows 40 buses assigned to the suburb and 60 to downtown, with no spare vehicles. If the suburb route gains 10 more buses, how many downtown buses are forgone?

options.misconception: adds instead of subtracting the shifted units
confuses total fleet with the marginal tradeoff

options.text: No buses are forgone because ridership rises

questions.explanation: With a fixed fleet of 100, shifting 10 buses to the suburb reduces downtown by 10. The forgone alternative is the opportunity cost.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A planner models 100 labor hours producing either 50 bus-miles or 25 sidewalk-miles. What is the opportunity cost of one sidewalk-mile in bus-miles?
questions.explanation: Dividing 50 bus-miles by 25 sidewalk-miles gives 2 bus-miles per sidewalk-mile. The ratio is constant here, so the cost is 2.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Describe a shift of the frontier
questions.stem: Explain how buying new electric buses could shift a transit planner's production possibilities frontier outward over time.

answer.exemplar: New electric buses raise the capital stock, so the same labor hours can produce more bus-miles or sidewalks; the frontier shifts outward, representing economic growth rather than a movement along it.

questions.explanation: Investment in capital expands productive capacity. A movement along the frontier reflects reallocation; an outward shift reflects growth.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The board runs every route at full capacity with no idle buses, yet riders complain of too few downtown routes. Which statement fits?

options.text: Both efficient, since no bus sits idle
options.misconception: assumes full capacity means optimal mix

options.text: Neither efficient, because complaints prove waste
options.misconception: treats feedback as evidence of idle resources

options.text: Productively efficient but possibly allocatively inefficient

questions.explanation: Full capacity with no idle buses is productive efficiency. Complaints about route mix suggest allocative inefficiency may coexist, so only productive efficiency is assured.
questions.hint: Full capacity signals productive efficiency; mix may still be off.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A planner has $100,000, buses cost $10,000 each and shelters $5,000 each. What is the maximum number of buses if zero shelters are bought?
questions.explanation: Dividing $100,000 by $10,000 per bus gives 10 buses. The budget constraint intercept is found by spending all funds on one good.
questions.hint: Spend the whole budget on buses.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Choosing to fund a new bike lane means delaying a rail station by two years. What does this decision demonstrate?

options.text: Scarcity only, with no cost to the delayed project
options.misconception: thinks scarcity exists without opportunity cost

options.text: Tradeoffs, because selecting one project delays another
Efficiency, because delay lowers construction costs
Growth, because bike lanes always raise output

questions.explanation: Selecting one use of limited funds delays another, which is the essence of a tradeoff. Scarcity underlies it but the demonstrated concept is tradeoffs.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: The board's five-year plan shows capital spending rising from $2 million to $3 million while maintenance stays flat. What is the most likely long-run effect?

options.misconception: assumes new capital needs no upkeep

options.text: Higher future service capacity from added capital
No change, because spending is just accounting
options.misconception: treats real investment as a bookkeeping entry

questions.explanation: Rising capital spending expands future productive capacity. It does not automatically cut fares, eliminate maintenance, or have no effect.
questions.hint: Investment adds to future capacity, not current consumption.

options.text: A surplus of riders causing inflation
Efficiency, because all drivers are working
options.misconception: equates working drivers with optimal allocation

options.text: Scarcity of drivers relative to desired service

questions.explanation: When desired service exceeds available drivers, drivers are scarce. Full employment of drivers is efficiency, not the scarcity itself.
questions.hint: Compare available drivers with desired routes.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS

answer.exemplar: The money is a transfer of funds, but the true cost is the next-best project foregone, which is the rail station delayed by two years.

questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative foregone, not the accounting expense. The delayed rail station is that alternative.
questions.hint: Focus on what is given up, not the price tag.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS

questions.stem: If 100 hours yield 40 bus-miles or 20 sidewalk-miles, how many bus-miles are sacrificed for 5 sidewalk-miles?
questions.explanation: The tradeoff is 2 bus-miles per sidewalk-mile, so 5 sidewalk-miles cost 10 bus-miles. Multiply the per-unit cost by the quantity.
